title: How Informed are the Swiss about Covid-19 and Prevention Measures? Results of a Survey on Information Awareness, Behaviour, and Deficits
screen_reason: Online quota survey of 1,129 Swiss inhabitants in April 2021. Among other measures, respondents answered a closed ordinal item on how often they had personally encountered Covid-19 misinformation ('fake news') since the pandemic began (Hourly / Daily / Weekly / Monthly / Semiannually / Never). The paper reports the share above two thresholds - 25% at least daily and 40% at least once a week - which are self-reported exposure shares of respondents, i.e. RECALL with recall_subtype = exposure. Note the paper's other misinformation measures (whether respondents correctly classified prevention measures) are BELIEF and are excluded by the protocol.

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific (general self-reported encounters, any channel)
estimates.date: April 2021 (respondents asked about encounters 'since the pandemic began', i.e. since March 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of Swiss respondents who said they encountered Covid-19 misinformation at least once a week since the pandemic began
estimates.denominator: 1,129 Swiss inhabitants surveyed online in April 2021 through a survey institute, quota-sampled on language region, age (18-74), gender and education
estimates.definition: Respondent chose Hourly, Daily or Weekly on the ordinal item 'Misinformation (fake news) about COVID-19 that I have encountered myself so far' (response options: Hourly, Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Semiannually, Never)
estimates.misinfo_def: Given the difficulty of knowing or assessing the reasons or intentions behind dissemination, we use the term misinformation throughout this study to refer broadly to any type of false information - including disinformation (see also Brennen et al., 2020).
estimates.source_quote: Furthermore, 25% of respondents said they encountered Covid-19 misinformation at least daily - 40% at least once a week since the pandemic began. Only 14% said they had not perceived/noted any misinformation (yet).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Subjectively Perceived Misinformation Regarding Covid-19', p. 132; item wording in Table 1 'Frequency of misinformation encounters', p. 128
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Purely subjective: the respondent decides what counted as misinformation, with no verification. The authors label the construct 'subjectively perceived misinformation' throughout and demonstrate its fallibility - of the 1,443 misinformation instances respondents volunteered in the open question, 68 were actually true statements. The reported intercoder reliability (a trained coder assistant's coding compared against a master coding of 10% of the material by the PI, rH > .83) applies to the content analysis of the OPEN answers, not to this closed frequency item.
estimates.moderator_quote: Frequency of misinformation encounters | Misinformation (fake news) about COVID-19 that I have encountered myself so far | Ordinal scale | Hourly / Daily / Weekly / Monthly / Semiannually / Never
estimates.notes: The 40% band nests the 25% daily band (at-least-weekly includes at-least-daily), so the two rows for this paper are threshold variants of one item and must not be summed. denom_scope = population per the survey rule. Denominator ambiguity: the paper says '40% of respondents' without restating the base; the regression on this item reports F(10, 1009) and a related ANOVA F(1, 1051), which implies roughly 1,020-1,053 valid answers rather than the full 1,129, so the true denominator may be slightly smaller than recorded. No channel is specified in the item, so the estimate is cross-platform self-reported encounter, not platform-specific.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) '86% encountered misinformation' WAS NOT RECORDED although it is tempting. The paper states only 'Only 14% said they had not perceived/noted any misinformation (yet)'; 100 - 14 is exactly the computed complement that R8 forbids, and the 14% row itself has an absence numerator (respondents who did NOT encounter), so no row was created either way. An adjudicator wanting an 'any encounter' figure should treat 14%-never as the source and flag the derivation. 2) BELIEF MEASURES EXCLUDED by the protocol ('Belief in false claims does NOT' count): 'ineffective measures were listed incorrectly as effective 214 times by 136 people (13%), and effective measures were falsely named as ineffective 408 times by 286 people (27%)'. These are shares of respondents holding a false belief about prevention measures, not exposure to misinformation, so they are not RECALL and not CONTENT. This is the main judgement call in this paper: 13% and 27% are the kind of percentages that look extractable but are belief, not encounter. 3) NOT A CONTENT ROW: 'respondents mentioned 1,443 instances of misinformation, 68 of which were actually found to be true statements'. 68/1,443 = 4.7% would be an exact part/whole share, but the construct is the error rate of respondents' own misinformation identification inside a respondent-generated set - an accuracy-of-perception metric, not the prevalence of misinformation in any population of items or people. Recorded here in case the review wants it as a self-report validity indicator. 4) COUNTS WITHOUT USABLE DENOMINATORS (mentions, not respondents), so no rows: content of the misinformation named - virus origin n = 195 (incl. 'Bill Gates invented/spread the virus' n = 43), 'the virus is harmless' n = 157, 'the virus does not exist' n = 83, deaths/infection rates n = 182, vaccination n = 167, various protective and curative products n = 133, a conspiracy of those in power n = 128, 'the virus came from a lab' n = 115, masks n = 103, contagion/transmissibility n = 71, preventive interventions n = 50, tests n = 28. Sources of the misinformation encountered (RQ3b): social media n = 197, news media n = 186, the internet in general n = 119, TV n = 100, politicians n = 93, friends and family n = 72. The paper never gives the base for these counts (they are mentions across 1,443 instances, and respondents could give several), so no share is derivable. 5) NOT MISINFORMATION MEASURES: RQ1 information-deficit shares (84% could name an underreported issue; vaccination and side effects n = 198, 17%; etc.) and RQ2 prevention-measure shares (93% named effective measures; social distancing n = 745, 66%; masks n = 665, 59%; hygiene n = 491, 44%; vaccination n = 290, 26%). 6) FIGURES CITED FROM OTHER SOURCES were excluded per R8, notably Nielsen et al. (2021): '30% of the respondents declared that they had encountered a lot or a great deal of false or misleading information about Covid-19 on social media in the past week' across eight countries (Switzerland not included) and 35% concern centred on political actors; also De Gani et al. (2021) 49% low health literacy, 72% difficulty with digital information; Friemel et al. (2021) 89% mask willingness, 63% social distancing willingness in April 2021. 7) MODERATOR ASSOCIATIONS reported without extractable shares: encounter frequency rose with education (r = .15, p < .01) and with use of scientific (r = .16) and popular science magazines (r = .20), and fell with TV use (r = -.11); men encountered misinformation more often than women (F(1, 1051) = 14.62, f = .12); the multiple regression explained only 8% of the variance in encounter frequency (F(10, 1009) = 9.05, R-squared = 0.082). H3.1 (social media use raises encounters) was NOT supported. 8) The article is from the European Journal of Health Communication 2022, Vol. 3(3) 118-142 - the Scopus id in the manifest is a later indexing record; the text is the correct paper.

rob.design: Online cross-sectional survey fielded through a survey institute in April 2021, N = 1,129 Swiss inhabitants. Quota sampling on Swiss population statistics: language region (n = 741 German-speaking, n = 387 French-speaking - note these sum to 1,128, one short of the stated N, and the Italian-speaking region is not covered), age (M = 48, SD = 15; 18-29 n = 160/14.2%, 30-39 n = 189/16.7%, 40-49 n = 227/20.1%, 50-59 n = 254/22.5%, 60-74 n = 299/26.5%, so 75+ is excluded), gender (n = 592 female, 52.4%) and education (low n = 91/8.1%, medium n = 568/50.3%, high n = 470/41.6%). NO RESPONSE RATE is reported and the sample is a quota, not probability, sample. Three open questions were content-analysed by one trained coder assistant using Mayring-style combined inductive/deductive coding; intercoder reliability was checked by comparing the assistant's coding against a master coding of 10% of the material by the PI, rH > .83 - a single-coder design with partial verification, and that check does not cover the closed frequency item used for the two extracted estimates. The exposure estimate rests on a single self-report ordinal item with no verification and a very long, vaguely bounded recall window ('so far' / 'since the pandemic began', about 13 months). Validated scales were used for the covariates (SciPop Cronbach's alpha = .89; Science Barometer Switzerland items; COSMO wave 32 items). Ethics approval obtained from the first author's university.
